questions.questionText: What is Machine Learning? Explain how it works and how it differs from traditional rule-based programming in your own words.
questions.referenceAnswer: Machine Learning is a subset of artificial intelligence where algorithms learn patterns directly from data rather than following hardcoded, explicit rules. In traditional programming, humans write explicit logic and input data to produce answers. In machine learning, algorithms receive data and known answers to learn the underlying rules or mathematical patterns. The process involves training on historical data, evaluating on validation sets, and generalizing to make predictions on unseen data.

importantConcepts.name: Learning from Data
importantConcepts.description: Algorithms deduce rules or statistical patterns from data rather than hand-coded logic.

importantConcepts.name: Contrast with Traditional Programming
importantConcepts.description: Rules + Data = Answers vs Data + Answers = Rules/Model.

importantConcepts.name: Training and Generalization
importantConcepts.description: Iterative parameter adjustment during training to accurately predict on unseen data.

importantConcepts.name: Feature Extraction / Pattern Recognition
importantConcepts.description: Identifying relevant features or patterns to map inputs to targets.

questions.questionText: Explain how a Hash Table operates, how it achieves average O(1) time complexity for lookups, and how collisions are handled.
questions.referenceAnswer: A hash table is a key-value data structure that achieves average O(1) constant time complexity for insertions, deletions, and lookups. It works by taking a key and passing it through a hash function that computes an integer index corresponding to a slot in an underlying array. When two distinct keys hash to the same bucket index, a collision occurs. Common collision resolution strategies include separate chaining (storing colliding items in linked lists or balanced trees at the bucket) and open addressing (such as linear or quadratic probing to find the next available array slot).

importantConcepts.name: Hash Function & Bucket Indexing
importantConcepts.description: Deterministic function mapping arbitrary keys to array index integers.

importantConcepts.name: Average O(1) Constant Time
importantConcepts.description: Direct array indexing allows instantaneous lookups without linear scanning.

importantConcepts.name: Collision Handling Mechanisms
importantConcepts.description: Resolution via separate chaining (linked lists) or open addressing (probing).

importantConcepts.name: Load Factor and Resizing
importantConcepts.description: Dynamic resizing when the table fills up to prevent performance degradation to O(n).

questions.questionText: Explain the biological process of Photosynthesis. Detail what occurs in the light-dependent reactions versus the light-independent Calvin cycle.
questions.referenceAnswer: Photosynthesis is the biochemical process by which autotrophs convert sunlight, water, and carbon dioxide into chemical energy in the form of glucose, releasing oxygen as a byproduct. In the light-dependent reactions within thylakoid membranes, chlorophyll absorbs photons, splitting water molecules (photolysis) to generate ATP, NADPH, and oxygen gas. In the light-independent Calvin cycle occurring in the stroma, the enzyme RuBisCO fixes atmospheric CO2 using the stored ATP and NADPH chemical energy to synthesize high-energy carbohydrates (glucose).

importantConcepts.name: Overall Energy Conversion & Equation
importantConcepts.description: Conversion of sunlight + CO2 + H2O into glucose (C6H12O6) and O2.

importantConcepts.name: Light-Dependent Reactions (Thylakoids)
importantConcepts.description: Photon absorption by chlorophyll, water photolysis, generation of ATP and NADPH.

importantConcepts.name: Calvin Cycle / Carbon Fixation (Stroma)
importantConcepts.description: Use of ATP/NADPH energy and RuBisCO to fix carbon dioxide into sugar molecules.

importantConcepts.name: Organelle Localization (Chloroplast)
importantConcepts.description: Thylakoid membranes versus stroma compartmentation.

questions.questionText: Describe the semi-conservative model of DNA replication. What are the key enzymes involved and how do leading and lagging strands differ?
questions.referenceAnswer: DNA replication is semi-conservative, meaning each newly formed double helix consists of one conserved template strand and one newly synthesized daughter strand. Key enzymes include Helicase (unwinds the replication fork), Primase (synthesizes RNA primers), DNA Polymerase (adds complementary nucleotides in the 5 to 3 direction and proofreads), and Ligase (seals phosphodiester backbone gaps). Because DNA polymerase only works in the 5 to 3 direction, the leading strand is synthesized continuously towards the fork, while the lagging strand is synthesized discontinuously away from the fork as Okazaki fragments that are subsequently joined by DNA ligase.

importantConcepts.name: Semi-Conservative Nature
importantConcepts.description: Each new double helix retains one parent strand and one synthesized strand.

importantConcepts.name: Key Replication Enzymes
importantConcepts.description: Roles of Helicase, DNA Polymerase, Primase, and DNA Ligase.

importantConcepts.name: Directionality and Strand Asymmetry
importantConcepts.description: Synthesis occurs strictly 5 prime to 3 prime.

importantConcepts.name: Leading vs. Lagging (Okazaki Fragments)
importantConcepts.description: Continuous synthesis vs discontinuous fragments joined by ligase.

questions.questionText: Explain Newton's Third Law of Motion. Why do action and reaction forces not simply cancel each other out?
questions.referenceAnswer: Newton's Third Law states that for every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction; whenever object A exerts a force on object B, object B exerts an equal magnitude force in the exact opposite direction on object A. These forces never cancel each other out to prevent acceleration because action-reaction pairs act on two completely different objects, not on the same body. For example, when you walk, your foot pushes backward on the ground, and the ground pushes forward on your foot; the forward force accelerates you, while the backward force slightly acts on the Earth.

importantConcepts.name: Equal and Opposite Force Pairs
importantConcepts.description: Forces always occur in matched pairs equal in magnitude and opposite in vector direction.

importantConcepts.name: Action on Different Bodies
importantConcepts.description: Action and reaction forces act on separate objects, so they do not sum to zero on a single body.

importantConcepts.name: Real-world Physics Example
importantConcepts.description: Clear demonstration (e.g., walking, rocket propulsion, swimming, or jumping).

questions.questionText: Explain how the interaction between market supply and demand establishes equilibrium price and quantity, and what happens during a shortage or surplus.
questions.referenceAnswer: Market equilibrium occurs at the intersection of the downward-sloping demand curve and upward-sloping supply curve, where the quantity demanded by consumers precisely equals the quantity supplied by producers at the equilibrium price. If price is above equilibrium, quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded, creating a surplus; producers compete by cutting prices until balance is restored. If price is below equilibrium, quantity demanded exceeds supply, creating a shortage; buyers compete, bidding prices upward until the market clears.

importantConcepts.name: Market Equilibrium Point
importantConcepts.description: Intersection where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied with no tendency for change.

importantConcepts.name: Dynamics of Surplus
importantConcepts.description: Price above equilibrium leads to excess supply, downward price pressure.

importantConcepts.name: Dynamics of Shortage
importantConcepts.description: Price below equilibrium leads to excess demand, upward bidding on prices.

importantConcepts.name: Price Mechanism as Signal
importantConcepts.description: Price shifts signal resource allocation and incentivize buyer and seller behaviors.

assessments.questionText: What is Machine Learning? Explain how it works and how it differs from traditional rule-based programming in your own words.
assessments.transcription: Machine learning is basically where computers learn directly from data instead of a programmer coding every single rule by hand. In normal software, you write if-else rules and feed inputs to get outputs. But in machine learning, you give the system inputs along with example outputs, and the model figures out the mathematical patterns. It trains over many epochs and then it can predict on new unseen data.

assessments.questionText: Explain Newton's Third Law of Motion. Why do action and reaction forces not simply cancel each other out?
assessments.transcription: Newton's third law says for every action force there is an equal and opposite reaction force. People often wonder why things move if the forces are equal and opposite. The crucial thing is that the action force and reaction force act on two entirely different objects. For example, when a swimmer pushes back against the water, the water pushes forward on the swimmer. Because the forces act on different bodies, they don't cancel out on the swimmer.
